Learning Objectives
Identify the three primary classes of materials used as bearing surfaces in the hip.
Review the relative performance of each class of bearing materials with respect to tribologic,
chemical, and mechanical properties.
Discuss the trade-offs associated with different bearing materials and their manufacturing
treatments.
Identify the primary biologic reactions associated with each bearing material.

Bearing materials and their byproducts must be selected to be bioinert, wear-resistant,
mechanically robust (tough), and chemically stable. These functional requirements are
universal for all total hip arthroplasty (THA) applications.
Three classes of bearing materials have emerged with clinical heritage since the advent of THA:
polymers, metals, and ceramics. Each class has evolved in manufacturing and chemistry to
best address the functional requirements of the hip (Resources 1 and 2).
All bearing materials have trade-offs, and no single bearing material suited for every clinical
application.

Bearing Materials
Surgeons should remember key concepts in considering the biologic, tribologic,
mechanical, and chemical properties of a material. From a biologic perspective, a
biomaterial must be considered with respect to its bulk (mm3-scale), particulate matter
(sub-mm scale), and any byproducts from chemical changes (eg, oxidation; Table 1).
Tribology is the study of friction and wear. All bearing materials experience material loss
during use. Material loss may result in mechanical changes to the bearing, and the
evolved wear debris may have mechanical or biologic effects on the bearing. The key
mechanical property to understand is toughness, or the ability to absorb energy without
failure. Toughness can be evaluated according to resistance to forming a crack or
propagating that crack. Toughness is differentiated from hardness, which is the
resistance to deformation. Chemical stability relates to resistance to changing chemical
and structural composition, typically via oxidation reactions or, in ceramics, phase
changes.

Polyethylene in THA
Rationale—Ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) has been the preferred
polymer bearing for THA since Charnley’s first failed use of polytetrafluoroethylene
necessitated a change to a lower wear bearing. No material has a longer clinical heritage.1
(Resource 3)
UHWMPE is a long-chain homopolymer with a molecular weight of 2 to 5 million g/mol,
consisting of only a carbon backbone and single-hydrogen side groups: (C2H4)n.2
Pure UHWMPE is supplied as a very fine powder for consolidation into bulk form and
manufacturing. Implants can be molded directly to form, or they can be machined from bar or
sheet stock.
If a hydrogen is removed from the carbon backbone, a free radical (unpaired electron)
remains.

Oxidation is the result of sterilization.
Historically, most prosthetic components composed of UHMWPE were sterilized via gamma
irradiation in air at a radiation dose of 25 to 40 kGy.
Radiation produces free radicals by knocking hydrogen atoms off the carbon backbone.
Higher radiation results in higher free radical concentrations.
Free radicals can react with oxygen in a form of degradation. The resulting reaction leads to
decreased molecular weight and changed polymer structure.
Oxidation results in increased elastic modulus, decreased ductility, and decreased strength.
Oxidized material, if subjected to stress and cycles of use, is associated with cracking,
delamination, and/or fatigue failure, all of which result in gross failure of the bearing.
Free radicals on adjacent chains can react with one another to form cross-links between
chains. This reaction happens in varying degrees in all polymer irradiation scenarios, including
gamma irradiation in air and gamma irradiation-permeable barrier treatments.
Some polyethylene components were sterilized without radiation, using ethylene oxide or gas
plasma.
Wear—The wear rate of UHMWPE is highly multifactorial and is governed by the treatment of
the materials in contact, lubrication, and the manner in which the materials move relative to
one another.
Wear in its broadest definition is the removal of material and, therefore, may be the result of
material loss after oxidation (spalling or delamination) or the result of the designed
articulation between two surfaces.
Articulation wear in polymers can occur because of abrasive interactions or adhesive
interactions between two materials. This is known as adhesive/abrasive wear.
Mechanical properties
Toughness of UHMWPE is governed by the ability of polymer chains to reorganize
themselves in response to an applied stress.
Increased cross-linking leads to decreased toughness, with laboratory-reported toughness
reductions of as much as 50%.
Diminishing material properties with regard to fracture toughness have been an undesirable
byproduct of the new processes for manufacturing polyethylene.
Increased cross-linking leads to decreased wear rates with laboratory-reported reductions of
as much as tenfold over never-irradiated material.
Highly cross-linked polyethylene3

Because irradiation is known to decrease wear rates but increase the potential for oxidation,
methods have been introduced to reduce oxidative potential while promoting cross-linking.
The free radicals formed during irradiation are stimulated to react with one another before
they can react with oxygen.
Gamma or electron beam radiation at 50 to 100 kGy or more is used to create free radicals.
This increased level of irradiation beyond the historical sterilization dose has increased the
cross-linking of polyethylene and has improved its wear resistance.4,5
Free radicals are reduced or eliminated via postirradiation thermal treatments that stimulate
free radical interactions between chains. These treatments are termed remelting and
annealing and their differentiation is important.
Remelting and annealing currently are used by different manufacturers, and any further
addition of free radicals is avoided via a final sterilization process in ethylene oxide gas.
Superior wear performance of highly cross-linked UHMWPE has been tested extensively in
the laboratory setting and validated through clinical results.
Oxidation resistance of cross-linked materials has been shown to be superior to gamma
irradiation in air and gamma irradiation-permeable barrier materials.
Remelting—Polyethylene is changed from its partial crystalline state to its amorphous state. All
of the free radicals are eliminated during the cross-linking process. After remelting, the final
percentage of crystallinity of polyethylene is slightly lower than before remelting. This reduces
the fracture toughness/fatigue toughness resistance of polyethylene because crystals arrest
crack propagation.
Annealing—Polyethylene is heated to a temperature below its melting point, which avoids a
reduction in its crystallinity but leaves a greater number of residual free radicals. Concern
exists that this process will result in the oxidation of the polyethylene over time.
Volumetric wear
Measured by the volume of material lost from the polyethylene
Directly related to square of the radius of the head
Larger femoral head has greater volumetric wear
Linear wear
Measured by the distance the femoral head has penetrated into the liner
Smaller femoral head of same material will have larger linear wear
Next-generation UHMWPE (antioxidants)6
Because of trade-offs associated with thermal treatment after radiation-induced cross-linking
(eg, reduction in toughness), next-generation UHMWPE, including antioxidants, has been

introduced.
Incorporation of antioxidants into UHMWPE allows for cross-linking via radiation in the
absence of a postirradiation thermal treatment.
Clinical results show near-zero oxidation of antioxidant materials.
Clinical results show wear rates are very low and not differentiable from highly cross-linked
UHMWPE (thermally treated)
Osteolysis is the biologic failure mode most often associated with polymer wear3,7 (Resource
5).
Etiology—Osteolysis associated with hip arthroplasty results from particulate wear debris
generated by femoral head articulation with a polyethylene liner or other bearing
replacement surface. The host response to wear particles leads to osteoclast activation and
osteolysis.
Cellular biology of bone resorption—Loose implants are surrounded by a membrane
containing fibroblasts, macrophages, and inflammatory mediators (prostaglandin E2,
interleukin 1, interleukin 6, tumor necrosis factor alpha). The local macrophage response to
debris activates the inflammatory cascade. The response is influenced by particle size,
composition, and number (Figure 1).

Polyethylene in THA
At the scale of several microns and higher, UHMWPE biologically is almost completely
inert. The high molecular weight contributes to a semicrystalline nature, with crystallinity
(ordered arrangement of the carbon chains) helping deliver superior mechanical and
wear properties.

The initial steps of consolidation and manufacturing do not result in any chemical
interactions between adjacent polymer chains. Direct compression molding refers to
polyethylene powder that is converted by heat and pressure into a final product. The
alternative is machining ram extruded bar stock or compression-molded sheets of
polyethylene into the requisite shape. These manufacturing processes are clean, but not
sterile.
Free radicals are very reactive and can be measured via electron spin resonance, also
known as electron paramagnetic resonance. If two unpaired electrons from adjacent
chains react with each other, the chains chemically link and are cross-linked. If the
unpaired electron is exposed to oxygen, an oxidation reaction takes place. Antioxidants
can be exploited to protect the free radicals against additional reaction.
When and where oxidation occurs is a function of the sterilization and treatment
process. Oxygen may be found in the surrounding atmosphere if the sterile device
packaging does not create an impermeable barrier (gamma irradiation in air). Oxygen
cannot react with the device during shelf storage if a barrier package is employed
(gamma irradiation-permeable barrier). Regardless of exposure to oxygen during shelf
storage, oxygen is present in the body, and free-radical containing devices will oxidize
after implantation (in vivo oxidation). Regardless of the location at which it happens,
oxidative degradation of the polyethylene can be measured by the presence of oxygen
chemically incorporated into the polymer structure.
Never-irradiated polyethylene has inferior wear properties because any irradiation
induces the cross-linking of polyethylene, which enhances its wear resistance. Although
this material initially is more oxidatively stable, clinical evidence shows that absorbed
lipids or sterols can contribute to in vivo oxidation, even in the absence of free radicals.
Oxidation rates in the hip from this mechanism appear to be low.
Wear is a function of distance slide between interfacing materials. For any bearing, more
cycles of use, or longer distance slide results in higher amounts of material loss. Polymer
wear is a strong function of how the sliding occurs, including the forces in the joint and
the degree to which that sliding direction changes. Multidirectional sliding motion has

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000503
8/21

been shown to increase wear rates, and this motion predominates in the hip, particularly
in comparison to the knee.
Polymer wear occurs because molecular chains and crystallites align during sliding
between two surfaces and then are torn apart if those surfaces change sliding direction.
Cross-linking inhibits the alignment of the crystallites and reduces the ability for them
(aligned or not aligned) to be torn apart.
Chains that move past one another easily convey more ductility and toughness to the
polymer. Therefore, chains that are chemically bonded via cross-linking have less
ductility and less toughness. Because fracture requires a crack to propagate through a
material, stress concentrators and voids (such as notches or consolidation defects) can
decrease component toughness, and crack-arresting features (such as higher
crystallinity) can increase toughness.
Substantial wear reduction (55% to 95% lower than that with non–cross-linked
polyethylene) has been reported for cross-linked polyethylene; however, these data
were collected in trials that used various polyethylene treatments, some of which had no
cross-linking at all and others that had the standard cross-linking associated with
sterilization (produced with 25 to 40 kGy).4,5 This provides some insight into the wide
range of relative wear reductions reported with newer methods of making polyethylene.
Although the exact reduction in wear is a topic of debate, the consensus is that the
values are low and acceptable. A polyethylene wear rate of less than 0.1 mm per year is
associated with a very low risk of osteolysis. Most currently available implants with
polyethylene components have achieved this wear rate.
Because of the improved wear resistance of the new polyethylene treatments, larger
femoral head sizes can be implanted. In the past, larger femoral head sizes were
associated with an increased wear rate because of the increased sliding distance of the
head across the acetabular surface with each step. At short-term follow-up, the in vivo
wear rate with these larger heads has been considerably reduced with the newer
methods of making polyethylene.

Premature failures have occurred in rare instances in which the acetabular implant was
placed vertically, with thin polyethylene at its rim. This especially is a concern with
implants that have larger femoral head sizes with a thinner polyethylene acetabular
lining and high irradiation doses.
In the hip, oxidation of highly cross-linked UHMWPE has been substantially reduced
compared with gamma irradiation in air and gamma irradiation-permeable barrier
materials. Oxidation in remelted materials, although detectable, remains below clinically
relevant values likely to lead to fatigue failure; however, oxidation in first-generation
annealed materials has been shown to result in delamination and fatigue failure under
high stress conditions, such as neck impingement or subluxation. Oxidation in second-
generation (eg, sequentially cross-linked) annealed materials is measurable but has not
reached values of clinical concern in the hip; however, these values have been reached
in the knee in some patients.
Residual free radicals in UHMWPE are protected by antioxidants. The final material has
improved overall toughness in the absence of melting because the crystalline structure
has not been altered.
If antioxidants are incorporated into the polymer powder before consolidation, they are
present for the entire manufacturing process. These can be mixed in a solid state or in a
liquid state. If antioxidants are present during the irradiation process, they inhibit free
radicals. Therefore, a larger radiation dose is required to attain the same cross-link
density and, therefore, the same wear resistance. An alternative process that avoids this
increased radiation dose involves incorporating antioxidants in the liquid state into the
polymer bulk after consolidation.
Wear particles of 0.5 to 5.0 μm induce a maximal response. Although particle materials
matter, osteolysis may occur secondary to polyethylene, cement, metal, or ceramic wear
debris. Most particles produced in THA polymer wear are smaller than 1 μm and induce
a vigorous response if produced at a high-enough rate. Therefore, the wear rate of
polyethylene is highly correlated with the development of osteolysis. The historical wear
rate of 28-mm UHMWPE liners is 0.1 to 0.2 mm/yr. Polyethylene liner wear rates of less

Metal-on-Metal Prostheses
Rationale—Metal-on-metal use was premised on reduced wear. Metal-on-metal articulations
produce less volumetric wear than metal-on-polyethylene articulations and may reduce the
incidence of osteolysis-induced failure.1,3,6
Enthusiasm for the use of metal-on-metal articulations is tempered by concerns for generated
metal ion debris compared with standard metal-on-polyethylene or ceramic bearing surfaces.
Metal-on-metal lubrication theory
The wear characteristics of metal-on-metal prostheses generally are characterized by a run-
in wear rate that usually occurs in the first 1 million cycles and is followed by a uniform rate
of wear.
The overall volume of wear of metal-on-metal prosthetic joint surfaces has been related to
the presence of a minimum elastohydrodynamic fluid-film thickness for the mean operating
conditions of load, speed, viscosity, and elastic properties of the metals used in each
prosthesis, which is described by the lambda ratio.
Clearance is another factor that influences wear in metal-on-metal bearings and must be
optimized.
A larger femoral head diameter increases the entrainment velocity (ie, the speed with which
the fluid is brought into the joint), maximizing fluid-film lubrication. Even with an ideal head
diameter and clearance, mixed film lubrication likely most frequently occurs in vivo.
A decreasing contact patch to rim (CPR) distance has been shown to influence wear rates.
In vivo results did not realize the benefits suggested in theory and in vitro testing.
Metal bearings are associated with considerable clinical drawbacks.
Adverse local tissue reactions (ALTRs) have been noted in failed metal-on-metal THA implants
that produced osteolytic responses with persistent pain, the frequency of which is unknown
(Figure 2). ALTRs have been reported in painful and well-functioning prostheses. The degree
of implant wear has not yet been directly correlated with the severity of all ALTRs. ALTR is
associated with various local joint and tissue findings.

lymphocytes with the development of a typical immunologic response

involves the use of a large femoral head, with a substantially higher incidence in the latter
group.

the dispersal of these particles throughout the body

Metal-on-Metal Prostheses
The lambda ratio is the ratio of the thickness of the fluid-film to the composite root
mean square surface roughness. If the lambda ratio is 1 or less for a metal-on-metal
bearing, severe mixed lubrication conditions occur, which means that abrasive wear
occurs via direct contact of the two bearing surfaces. A lambda ratio of 3 or greater
indicates that fluid-film lubrication is adequate to substantially reduce the effect of load
and, therefore, minimize friction and wear. Lower clearance and larger femoral head
sizes promote higher lambda ratios.
In THA, clearance is the difference between the diameter of the femoral head and the
diameter of the acetabular cup, with clearances of 100 to 200 μm maximizing the fluid-
film thickness. These clearances maximize joint fluid entrapment between the two
bearing surfaces. Clearances that are too high result in increased wear and clearances
that are too low can result in clamping and/or equatorial seizing.
CPR distance is the distance between the point of application of the joint reaction force
and the rim of the acetabular implant in a patient in the standing position. An inverse
relationship exists between wear and CPR distance. The mean CPR distance is
approximately 14 mm. A CPR distance of less than 5 mm is associated with increased
metal ion levels and increased rates of prosthetic loosening, wear, and dislocation.
Factors that result in decreased CPR distance include a high abduction angle of the
acetabular implant, excessive anteversion of the acetabular cup, and cup designs with
smaller arcs of coverage of the femoral head.
Early in vivo data from the analysis of retrieved McKee-Farrar prostheses show mean
linear wear rates of 0.003 and 0.004 mm/yr for the femoral head and cup, respectively.8
Larger diameter (42 mm) femoral heads had a twofold lower mean volumetric wear rate

than smaller diameter (35 mm) femoral heads (0.7 mm3 versus 1.4 mm3 per year,
respectively).
Current-generation metal-on-metal bearings (high-carbon, wrought cobalt-chromium
alloy) with a 28-mm-diameter femoral head had a mean in vivo wear rate of 27.8 μm/yr
for the first year of use and 6.2 μm/yr after the second year, with femoral heads
generally exhibiting a higher wear rate than acetabular cups. A positive correlation
between clearance and wear rate also was observed.
Metal-on-metal bearings and corresponding metallic wear debris can release metallic
ions in substantially greater concentrations than those that typically occur with
polyethylene-covered or ceramic bearings, and these ions may form soluble or
precipitated organometallic substances.
Metal-on-metal wear debris particles are approximately 10 to 50 nm.
Corrosion, both mechanical and chemical, of the articular surfaces of a metal-on-metal
joint prosthesis leads to the production of metal ions (eg, Co2+), which are measured in
the tissues, blood, and urine. The concentrations of these ions currently are being
measured prospectively with resurfacing and stem-type hip devices and have been
found to be increased in all series in which they have been measured.
An early review of the incidence of cancer in patients with prostheses with metal-on-
metal bearings found that leukemia was the only cancer that may occur at an increased
rate in these patients. However, the follow-up period was only 5 to 14 years, and longer
follow-up times did not reveal any increased risk of hematopoietic cancers. More recent,
large population-based studies have shown no greater risk of hematopoietic or other
cancers at 7-year follow-up.9
Ceramic Bearings
Rationale—Ceramics as a class of materials are exceptionally hard, chemically and biologically
inert, and wear resistant.1,2,6

Bearing couples can include ceramic on polyethylene and ceramic on ceramic.
Materials—All-ceramic bearing materials generally have been designed around oxides of
aluminum and zirconium.
Alumina was the original ceramic used in arthroplasty.10
Zirconia was introduced as an alternative material to minimize the risk of fracture associated
with alumina but did not result in clinical success.
Zirconia-toughened alumina is stable and associated with higher clinical success than pure
zirconia.11,12
Ceramicized metals (eg, oxidized zirconium, oxidized titanium) exploit the hardness and wear
resistance of ceramics while maintaining toughness of metals and avoiding metal sensitivity
associated with nickel or chromium.13-15
Wear rates with ceramic bearings generally are low in laboratory and in vivo studies. This is
attributed to material hardness, decreased porosity, and ability to manufacture with tight
tolerances. Under certain circumstances, ceramics are not immune to clinically significant wear
rates.16-19
Biologically, the periprosthetic tissues in failed ceramic-on-ceramic prostheses have been
found to have thinner synovial layers, fewer macrophages, and lower production of osteolytic
substances than metal-on-polyethylene articular surfaces7 (Figure 3).
Disadvantages of ceramic bearings
Squeaking of ceramic-on-ceramic bearings has been reported in a small fraction of the
patient population.
Revision of ceramic prostheses after catastrophic fracture of a ceramic femoral head or
acetabular liner remains a difficult problem, with some studies reporting a prosthetic survival
rate of only 63% at 5 years because of aseptic loosening and osteolysis.20
Revision for a fractured ceramic bearing must include a complete synovectomy to remove
remnant ceramic particles that can cause third-body wear. Revision of the acetabular implant
is necessary if damage to the locking mechanism or component malpositioning is present. If
minimal damage to the femoral taper is present, the femoral stem may be retained and
revised with the use of a fourth-generation ceramic head with a titanium sleeve. If damage
beyond simple scratches or corrosion is present, then revision of the femoral implant is
necessary.
During revision for a fractured ceramic femoral head or liner, a ceramic-on-ceramic or
ceramic-on-polyethylene bearing should be used. Metal-on-polyethylene bearings should be
avoided to prevent third-body wear and femoral head erosion.

Ceramic Bearings
The alumina used in modern arthroplasty, Al2O3, is a dense, polycrystalline ceramic
obtained from aluminum oxide powder and pressed in a mold at a very high
temperature. Al2O3 is very stable and chemically inert. Although alumina is very resistant
to compression, it is brittle and susceptible to fracture. Recent analysis of clinical data
suggests a fracture rate of approximately 0.36% for alumina femoral heads and inserts
in THA implants.10
Dissimilar from alumina, zirconia needs to be chemically stabilized. Zirconia exists in
three distinct crystalline phases: monoclinic, tetragonal, and cubic. The phase changes
result in a greater variation in volume than that in alumina and substantially reduce its
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Total Hip Arthroplasty: Bearing Surfaces Basic Science
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000503
16/21

mechanical durability because of the occurrence of cracks. To maintain zirconia in its
most stable, tetragonal phase, yttrium oxides have been added to bond with the
zirconia, creating yttrium-stabilized tetragonal polycrystalline zirconia.
The clinical wear of zirconia on polyethylene has been found to be greater in vivo than
that predicted in vitro, with a mean wear of 0.17 mm/yr. This is substantially greater than
the wear of alumina on polyethylene, which is a mean of 0.07 mm/yr. Therefore, pure
zirconia implants are no longer used in THA.
Production of zirconia-toughened alumina involves homogeneous distribution of yttria-
stabilized tetragonal zirconia particles (24%) and strontium oxide to alumina (75%) to
prevent crack propagation. This theoretically maintains the wear properties of alumina
while decreasing the risk of fracture.
Clinical performance is reported as being very good. Reported fractures are
exceptionally low, and an in vitro study showed 6 to 12 times lower wear rates compared
with alumina bearings.11 Registry data show no substantial difference in revision rate for
as long as 7 years compared with metal on cross-linked polyethylene.12
The most modern oxidized zirconium material is produced via a process of thermally
treating zirconium metal and niobium to create a hard, smooth ceramic outer core. The
rest of the implant remains metal, which theoretically decreases fracture risk. Midterm in
vivo wear studies comparing this to ceramic and cobalt-chromium femoral heads have
report somewhat variable results; however, results generally are on par with metal on
UHMWPE.13-15
Ceramics are wettable materials. Clearances of 20 to 50 μm should be achieved during
the manufacturing process to provide optimal fluid-film lubrication. Similar to metal-on-
metal bearings, the alumina-alumina couple exhibits biphasic behavior, with run-in and
steady-state wear rates of 1.2 and 0.02 mm3 per million cycles, respectively.
The phenomenon of microseparation, leading to stripe wear, is a recent concern. This
usually is present on the femoral head, at which it potentially edge loads with the

Recent analysis of alumina wear debris has shown that it has a bimodal distribution, with
particle sizes of 5 to 90 nm and 0.05 to 3.2 μm. In general, a reduction in grain size and
porosity of the alumina correlates with a lower wear rate.19
Squeaking is indicative of a poorly lubricated articulation, and although it is not directly
linked to other clinical failure modes, patients find the noise objectionable. The incidence
in zirconia-toughened alumina is reported to be on par with prior generation ceramics,
at approximately 2%.
Risk factors for femoral head fracture include a small femoral head (28 mm) and a short
neck size. Risk factors for acetabular liner fracture include cup malpositioning (excessive
anteversion) and malalignment of the liner during insertion. Obesity is a risk factor for
both fractures.
